name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Geometry and bond angle of water

questiontext.text:
Observe the given gas-phase molecular structure of water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) showing the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond length and the unknown bond angle \(\theta\):

Identify the bond angle \(\theta\) and the molecular geometry of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) in the gas phase.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram represents a single \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecule in the gas phase with a central oxygen atom bonded to two terminal hydrogen atoms, an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond length of \(95.7\text{ pm}\), and an \(\mathrm{H-O-H}\) bond angle labeled \(\theta\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The molecule is treated as an isolated gas-phase species without intermolecular hydrogen bonding, so its geometry is governed by valence shell electron pair repulsion around the oxygen atom.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Oxygen has six valence electrons: two form single covalent bonds with hydrogen atoms and four remain as two lone pairs. According to VSEPR theory, four electron pairs adopt a tetrahedral arrangement, but lone pair–lone pair and lone pair–bond pair repulsions compress the bond angle below the ideal tetrahedral angle of \(109.5^\circ\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because of the two lone pairs on the oxygen atom, the two \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bonds are pushed closer together, giving a bent (V-shaped) geometry with an experimentally observed \(\mathrm{H-O-H}\) bond angle of \(104.5^\circ\) in the gas phase.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The angle \(104.5^\circ\) is smaller than \(109.5^\circ\) due to lone-pair repulsion and matches the bent structure of water. Thus, the bond angle \(\theta\) is \(104.5^\circ\) and the molecular geometry is bent.

answer.text: \(94.8^\circ\), linear
\(109.5^\circ\), tetrahedral
\(120.0^\circ\), trigonal planar

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Open-book structure of hydrogen peroxide

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the non-planar open-book structure of hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) in the gas phase:

What is the value of the dihedral angle \(\phi\) in the gas phase, and how does it change when \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is in the solid phase at \(110\text{ K}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the open-book geometry of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) in the gas phase with an \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bond length of \(147.5\text{ pm}\), an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond length of \(95.0\text{ pm}\), an \(\mathrm{H-O-O}\) bond angle of \(94.8^\circ\), and the dihedral angle between the two \(\mathrm{H-O-O}\) planes labeled \(\phi\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The dihedral angle \(\phi\) is the angle between the two half-planes containing the \(\mathrm{H-O-O}\) units intersecting along the \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bond axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Hydrogen peroxide adopts a non-planar structure to minimize repulsion between the lone pairs on the adjacent oxygen atoms. In the solid phase, intermolecular hydrogen bonding modifies the molecular dimensions compared to the isolated gas-phase molecule.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In the gas phase, the dihedral angle \(\phi\) is \(111.5^\circ\). Upon cooling to the solid phase at \(110\text{ K}\), crystal packing and hydrogen-bonding forces compress the dihedral angle from \(111.5^\circ\) down to \(90.2^\circ\) (while the \(\mathrm{H-O-O}\) angle increases from \(94.8^\circ\) to \(101.9^\circ\) and the \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bond length shortens slightly from \(147.5\text{ pm}\) to \(145.8\text{ pm}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking both phases confirms that the gas-phase dihedral angle is \(111.5^\circ\) and it decreases to \(90.2^\circ\) in the solid phase.

answer.text: \(111.5^\circ\); decreases to \(90.2^\circ\) in the solid phase
\(90.2^\circ\); increases to \(111.5^\circ\) in the solid phase
\(104.5^\circ\); remains unchanged in the solid phase
\(180.0^\circ\); decreases to \(101.9^\circ\) in the solid phase

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded unit in ice

questiontext.text:
The schematic below shows a local structural unit of hexagonal ice, where solid lines represent covalent \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bonds and dashed lines represent hydrogen bonds:

Based on this structural arrangement, how many nearest-neighbour oxygen atoms surround each oxygen atom tetrahedrally, and what is the primary structural consequence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows one central oxygen atom (green sphere) connected to four surrounding oxygen atoms, with hydrogen atoms (orange spheres) positioned along the lines joining the oxygen atoms. Each \(\mathrm{O}\cdots\mathrm{O}\) separation is \(276\text{ pm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In crystalline ice at atmospheric pressure (hexagonal form), each \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecule participates in hydrogen bonding through its two hydrogen atoms (donors) and two lone pairs on oxygen (acceptors).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
X-ray diffraction studies of ice crystals show that each oxygen atom is surrounded tetrahedrally by four other oxygen atoms at a distance of \(276\text{ pm}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Counting the nearest-neighbour oxygen atoms directly linked to the central oxygen atom gives four. Because directional hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in a rigid tetrahedral network, the lattice is not close-packed; instead, it forms an open-type three-dimensional structure containing wide empty spaces (holes). These holes increase the volume for a given mass, making the density of ice lower than that of liquid water.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This lower density explains why ice floats on water. Therefore, each oxygen atom is surrounded by four nearest-neighbour oxygen atoms, resulting in an open-type structure with wide holes and lower density than water.

answer.text: Two; ice becomes denser than liquid water
Six; ice forms a close-packed cubic lattice at atmospheric pressure
Four; ice acquires an open-type structure with wide holes and lower density than water
Eight; ice exhibits metallic conductivity at \(273\text{ K}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Industrial sources of dihydrogen production

questiontext.text:
The bar chart below represents the approximate percentage share of different raw-material sources in the industrial production of dihydrogen:

Identify Source P, Source Q, and Source R respectively.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The bar chart displays four industrial dihydrogen production shares: Source P at \(77\%\), Source Q at \(18\%\), Source R at \(4\%\), and Other sources at \(1\%\). Note that \(77\% + 18\% + 4\% + 1\% = 100\%\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The percentages represent the global/industrial breakdown of commercial dihydrogen production by feedstock/process.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Commercial dihydrogen is primarily manufactured by steam reforming of hydrocarbons (petrochemicals), coal gasification followed by the water-gas shift reaction, and electrolysis of aqueous solutions.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Matching the values to the industrial production data: approximately \(77\%\) of industrial dihydrogen is produced from petrochemicals (Source P), \(18\%\) from coal (Source Q), \(4\%\) from electrolysis of aqueous solutions (Source R), and \(1\%\) from other sources.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The order from largest to smallest among P, Q, and R is petrochemicals (\(77\%\)), coal (\(18\%\)), and electrolysis of aqueous solutions (\(4\%\)).

answer.text: Coal, petrochemicals, electrolysis of aqueous solutions
Electrolysis of aqueous solutions, coal, petrochemicals
Biomass gasification, petrochemicals, coal
Petrochemicals, coal, electrolysis of aqueous solutions

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Combustion energy comparison of fuels

questiontext.text:
The chart below compares the energy released on combustion per gram (\(\mathrm{kJ\,g^{-1}}\)) and per litre (\(\mathrm{kJ\,L^{-1}}\)) for four fuels:

Using the plotted data, if \(10\text{ kg}\) of fuel is combusted, how much more energy is released by gaseous dihydrogen compared to liquid octane, and why does liquid octane require far less storage volume for the same energy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the bar chart:
- Gaseous dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\)): \(143\text{ kJ g}^{-1}\) and \(12\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\).
- Liquid octane: \(47\text{ kJ g}^{-1}\) and \(34005\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\).
- Mass of each fuel combusted: \(m = 10\text{ kg} = 10{,}000\text{ g}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Complete combustion is assumed under the standard reference conditions used for the chart values.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\text{Total energy released } (E) = \text{mass (g)} \times \text{energy per gram (kJ g}^{-1}\text{)}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Energy from \(10{,}000\text{ g}\) of gaseous \(\mathrm{H}_2\):
\[E_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 10{,}000\text{ g} \times 143\text{ kJ g}^{-1} = 1{,}430{,}000\text{ kJ} = 1.43 \times 10^6\text{ kJ}\]
2. Energy from \(10{,}000\text{ g}\) of liquid octane:
\[E_{\text{octane}} = 10{,}000\text{ g} \times 47\text{ kJ g}^{-1} = 470{,}000\text{ kJ} = 4.70 \times 10^5\text{ kJ}\]
3. Difference in energy released:
\[\Delta E = 1.43 \times 10^6\text{ kJ} - 4.70 \times 10^5\text{ kJ} = 9.60 \times 10^5\text{ kJ}\]
4. Comparing volumetric energy density: liquid octane releases \(34005\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\), whereas gaseous dihydrogen releases only \(12\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\), so liquid octane stores vastly more energy per unit volume.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
On a mass-for-mass basis, dihydrogen releases about three times more energy than octane (\(143 / 47 \approx 3.04\)), giving \(9.6 \times 10^5\text{ kJ}\) more energy for \(10\text{ kg}\) of fuel, while octane's much higher volumetric energy density (\(34005\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\) vs \(12\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\)) makes its storage far more compact.

answer.text: \(4.7 \times 10^5\text{ kJ}\) more; octane has lower energy per mole
\(9.6 \times 10^5\text{ kJ}\) more; octane has a much higher energy density per litre (\(34005\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\) vs \(12\text{ kJ L}^{-1}\))
\(1.43 \times 10^6\text{ kJ}\) more; gaseous dihydrogen has higher energy per litre
\(2.86 \times 10^5\text{ kJ}\) more; octane has a higher energy per gram

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Isotopic trends in hydrogen properties

questiontext.text:
The chart below summarizes key physical properties of the isotopic diatomic molecules \(\mathrm{H}_2\), \(\mathrm{D}_2\), and \(\mathrm{T}_2\):

Which conclusion is best supported by the plotted data?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The chart provides the boiling points of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) (\(20.39\text{ K}\)), \(\mathrm{D}_2\) (\(23.67\text{ K}\)), and \(\mathrm{T}_2\) (\(25.0\text{ K}\)), along with the bond dissociation enthalpies at \(298.2\text{ K}\) for \(\mathrm{H}_2\) (\(435.88\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and \(\mathrm{D}_2\) (\(443.35\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Isotopes of hydrogen have the same electronic configuration (\(1\mathrm{s}^1\)) and therefore undergo similar chemical reactions, with differences in rates governed by bond dissociation enthalpies and differences in physical properties governed by mass.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A higher bond dissociation enthalpy means more energy is required to break the covalent bond in the rate-determining step, leading to a slower reaction rate. Meanwhile, increasing molar mass among isotopic molecules increases the boiling point.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the values:
- Bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{D}_2\) (\(443.35\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is greater than that of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) (\(435.88\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), so \(\mathrm{D}_2\) reacts slower than \(\mathrm{H}_2\).
- Boiling point increases monotonically from \(\mathrm{H}_2\) (\(20.39\text{ K}\)) to \(\mathrm{D}_2\) (\(23.67\text{ K}\)) to \(\mathrm{T}_2\) (\(25.0\text{ K}\)) as the isotopic mass increases.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both trends are directly verified from the plotted values: \(\mathrm{D}_2\) reacts slower than \(\mathrm{H}_2\) due to its higher bond dissociation enthalpy, and the boiling point increases with isotopic mass.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{D}_2\) reacts slower than \(\mathrm{H}_2\) due to its higher bond dissociation enthalpy (\(443.35\) vs \(435.88\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), and boiling point increases with isotopic mass
\(\mathrm{H}_2\) reacts slower than \(\mathrm{D}_2\) because \(\mathrm{H}_2\) has a higher enthalpy of fusion
\(\mathrm{T}_2\) has the lowest boiling point because tritium is radioactive
\(\mathrm{H}_2\) and \(\mathrm{D}_2\) have identical bond dissociation enthalpies because their internuclear distance is \(74.14\text{ pm}\)
